intro: Searching for the best family trust near me usually means you want to protect family assets, plan for inheritance tax, or make sure the right people manage money for your family's future. You are likely looking for a wills and probate specialist who can explain how trusts work and help you set one up properly. iComply introduces you to a suitable UK professional who will quote you directly, with fees on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a family trust usually need
need_lead: A family trust can be a useful way to hold assets for your family, but the right approach depends on your circumstances.
needs: You want to set up a trust to hold money or property for your children or grandchildren, with clear rules about when and how they benefit.
You are worried about inheritance tax and want to understand whether a trust could help reduce the tax your family might face.
You need help choosing trustees who will manage the trust responsibly and in line with your wishes.
You are unsure which type of trust suits your family situation and need advice on the tax treatment of different trusts.
You have been named as a trustee and want to understand your duties, including registering the trust with HMRC where required.
context: Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated. Solicitors regulated by the SRA and chartered legal executives regulated by CILEx are insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman, and many specialists are also members of STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly.

Trusts usually need to be registered with HMRC, and different trusts have different tax treatment. When choosing a professional, ask whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance, and where your original will is stored. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Explain what you want the trust to achieve, such as protecting family wealth or planning for inheritance tax.
Mention who you expect to benefit from the trust and whether they are children, grandchildren or others.
Say whether you already have a will and whether it needs to be updated alongside the trust.
Describe any assets you are considering putting into the trust, such as savings, investments or property.
Confirm where in the UK you live, as the rules differ in Scotland.
Note whether you have any particular concerns about choosing trustees or registering the trust with HMRC.
questions: Are you regulated, and do you hold professional indemnity insurance?
Which type of trust would you recommend for my family situation, and why?
How will the trust be taxed, and what do I need to do about registering it with HMRC?
Who should I choose as trustees, and what are their responsibilities?
Will setting up a trust affect my will, and do I need to update it?
What are your fees, and how will you keep me informed as the trust is set up?

faqs.q: Do I need a solicitor to set up a family trust?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but trusts can be complex and the tax rules vary. Using a regulated professional such as a solicitor or chartered legal executive can help ensure the trust is set up correctly and that you understand your obligations.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a family trust and a will?
faqs.a: A will sets out what happens to your assets when you die, while a trust can hold assets for beneficiaries during your lifetime or after your death. Many people use both together as part of their estate planning.

faqs.q: How do I choose the best professional for a family trust?
faqs.a: There is no single definition of best, so look for someone regulated, insured and experienced in trusts. Ask about their approach, fees and whether they are a member of a specialist body such as STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly.

faqs.q: Does a family trust need to be registered with HMRC?
faqs.a: Most trusts now need to be registered with HMRC's Trust Registration Service, although there are some exceptions. The professional you speak to can confirm whether your trust needs to be registered and help you do it.

extra_heading: Narrowing down the best family trust near you
extra: The words "best" and "near me" tell us two things: you want someone who genuinely knows family trusts, and you would rather deal with a professional you can sit down with locally. There is no official ranking of best, so the sensible approach is to compare on what you can check — regulation, insurance, trust experience and clear fees — rather than on any label. Being nearby also matters in practice, because setting up a trust often runs alongside updating your will, and you may want to discuss trustees and beneficiaries face to face.

When you speak to a professional, ask how they would approach your particular family situation rather than accepting a general description of trusts. A good first conversation should cover which type of trust might suit you, how it would be taxed, and who should act as trustees, since trustees carry real responsibilities. It is also worth asking how the trust fits with your will, so the two documents work together rather than pulling in different directions.

Expect the first appointment to be a fact-finding discussion: your assets, who you want to benefit, and what you are trying to protect or plan for. You do not need to have decided anything before that meeting, and it is fine to take notes and go away to think. Because fees are quoted on application, ask early what the professional charges and how they will keep you informed as the work progresses.

extra_faqs.q: Can I compare family trust professionals on price alone?
extra_faqs.a: Price is only part of the picture, because trusts vary in complexity and the tax treatment differs between types. Compare what is included, whether the professional is regulated and insured, and how clearly they explain the options before you decide.

extra_faqs.q: Should the same professional set up my trust and update my will?
extra_faqs.a: It often makes sense, because a trust and a will need to work together and a single adviser can see the whole picture. If you use different people, make sure each knows what the other is doing so the documents do not conflict.

extra_faqs.q: What if I live in Scotland?
extra_faqs.a: Succession and confirmation follow their own rules in Scotland, so check that any adviser you speak to practises in the right jurisdiction. Mention where you live when you enquire so you are introduced to someone suited to your situation.
